# Best Broadway Shows from 2020

As we look back from March 2026, the Broadway shows that opened in 2020 represent a fascinating snapshot of a season cut dramatically short. Before the pandemic shuttered theaters that spring, these productions captured a moment of artistic ambition and reinvention on Broadway stages.

Leading our selection is **Les Misérables**, which earns an 83/100 score for its grittier reimagining at the refurbished Sondheim Theatre. This rebooted production takes a darker, more visceral approach to the beloved musical, winning over most critics even as some purists remain unconvinced by the radical departure from tradition.

**A Soldier's Play** stands as another highlight, bringing Charles Fuller's Pulitzer Prize-winning drama to Broadway for the first time in a powerful revival that scores 78/100. The production demonstrates how this examination of racism and violence within a segregated Army unit remains urgently relevant, with critics praising both the stellar performances and the long-overdue Broadway recognition for Fuller's work.

The season also features Ivo van Hove's polarizing **West Side Story** reimagining, which divides critics with its bold visual design and unconventional staging choices, and **My Name is Lucy Barton**, where Laura Linney's luminous solo performance elevates Elizabeth Strout's intimate novel to mixed critical reception.

With an average score of 75/100 across these five productions, the brief 2020 season showcased Broadway's ongoing tension between honoring classics and pushing theatrical boundaries. Whether you're drawn to ambitious reinventions or intimate character studies, these shows offer a glimpse of where Broadway was headed before an unprecedented interruption reshaped the industry.

The ten highest-rated shows from 2021 average an impressive 81/100 critic score, reflecting a year that prioritized artistic ambition alongside commercial appeal. Leading the pack is **Dana H.**, Lucas Hnath's unconventional docudrama featuring Deirdre O'Connell's mesmerizing lip-sync performance to interviews with Hnath's mother about her harrowing kidnapping. Critics consistently describe it as unforgettable, pushing theatrical boundaries in ways few productions dare.

The experimental spirit extends to **Is This a Room**, which transforms a verbatim FBI transcript of Reality Winner's interrogation into gripping theater, and **Pass Over**, Antoinette Chinonye Nwandu's urgent drama that appropriately became Broadway's first show back after the shutdown. Meanwhile, **The Lehman Trilogy** demonstrates that epic scale and intimate storytelling can coexist, with three actors charting 163 years of American capitalism.

The list also showcases Broadway's range, from Andrew Lloyd Webber's long-running **The Phantom of the Opera** to innovative revivals like the gender-swapped **Company** and the immersive **Cabaret at the Kit Kat Club**. Solo performances shine in **Lackawanna Blues**, while **SIX** proves that pop-concert energy can fuel theatrical storytelling.

Whether you're seeking experimental theater, reimagined classics, or spectacular musicals, the 2021 season offers productions that continue to reward audiences with their artistic vision and theatrical craft.

Leading our selection is a grittier reimagining of **Les Misérables** at the refurbished Sondheim Theatre, earning an 83/100 from critics who largely embrace its darker, rebooted approach, though the production doesn't win over everyone. Close behind, **A Soldier's Play** makes its long-overdue Broadway debut with a stellar revival that proves Charles Fuller's Pulitzer-winning drama remains as urgent and relevant as ever, examining racism and power within a World War II-era Black regiment.

The season also brings **Grand Horizons**, a boulevard comedy about a divorcing elderly couple that critics find pleasant if familiar, elevated significantly by the performances of Jane Alexander and James Cromwell. Meanwhile, Laura Linney commands the stage solo in **My Name is Lucy Barton**, an adaptation that divides critics even as they universally praise her luminous performance. Rounding out our top five, Ivo van Hove's radical **West Side Story** reimagining proves deeply divisive, with some critics celebrating its bold vision while others question its departures from the beloved original.

With an average critic score of 75/100 across these five productions, the 2020 season demonstrates Broadway's ongoing tension between honoring theatrical legacy and pushing boundaries. Whether you're drawn to bold reinterpretations or powerful dramatic revivals, these productions offer multiple entry points into the year's theatrical conversation.

best-broadway-plays-2021.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays That Opened in 2021

As we look back from March 2026, the 2021 Broadway season stands as a watershed moment in theatrical history—the industry's dramatic return following an unprecedented 18-month pandemic shutdown. The plays that premiered that year captured both the urgency of reopening and a creative boldness that continues to resonate with audiences today.

Among the standout productions, **Dana H.** remains one of the most unconventional and daring works to grace a Broadway stage. Deirdre O'Connell's extraordinary lip-sync performance to a real interview transcript creates an unsettling docudrama that critics describe as mesmerizing and unforgettable. Equally experimental, **Is This a Room** transforms a verbatim FBI transcript into a pulse-pounding thriller that proves documentary theater can be as gripping as any fictional drama.

The season also delivered powerful solo performances, with **Lackawanna Blues** showcasing Ruben Santiago-Hudson's virtuosic ability to embody dozens of characters from his childhood, and urgent contemporary work like **Pass Over**, which appropriately served as Broadway's official reopening production with its potent examination of Black American experience.

Epic storytelling found its place too, particularly in **The Lehman Trilogy**, which traces 160 years of American capitalism through one family's rise and fall. Meanwhile, bold reinterpretations of classics—from a gender-swapped **Company** to an immersive **Cabaret at the Kit Kat Club**—demonstrated that traditional musicals could feel radically fresh.

With an impressive average critic score of 81/100 across these ten productions, the 2021 season proved that Broadway could return not just with spectacle, but with substance and innovation. As we look back from March 2026, the Broadway season of 2022 stands out as a remarkable year that brought fresh voices and celebrated revivals to the stage in equal measure. The year's offerings span from intimate one-person shows to sweeping ensemble pieces, with several Pulitzer Prize winners making their Broadway debuts or returns. **Kimberly Akimbo** leads the pack with near-universal critical acclaim for its delicate balance of humor and heartbreak, proving that quirky, character-driven musicals can achieve both commercial and artistic success. Close behind, **Into the Woods** demonstrates how a stripped-down approach to classic material can feel both reverent and revelatory, serving as a fitting tribute to Stephen Sondheim's legacy. Meanwhile, **A Strange Loop** breaks new ground entirely with Michael R. Jackson's brazenly original meta-musical that challenges theatrical conventions while earning widespread critical praise.

The list also highlights Broadway's commitment to reviving essential American plays, with new productions of Suzan-Lori Parks's **Topdog/Underdog** and Paula Vogel's **How I Learned to Drive** proving these works' enduring power and relevance. Tom Stoppard's **Leopoldstadt** rounds out the dramatic offerings with a deeply personal meditation on history and identity.

Whether you're exploring these shows through recordings, published scripts, or hoping to catch any still-running productions, this collection represents a snapshot of Broadway firing on all cylinders—diverse, daring, and deeply human.

best-broadway-plays-2023.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays of 2023

As we look back from March 2026, the plays that opened on Broadway in 2023 represent one of the most critically acclaimed seasons in recent memory, with an average critic score of 82/100 across our top ten selections.

The year proved particularly remarkable for revivals that found fresh urgency in classic material. **Merrily We Roll Along** stands as the crown jewel of the season, with Maria Friedman's production finally unlocking the emotional power of Sondheim and Furman's notorious 1981 flop through intimate staging and deeply felt performances. **Appropriate**, Branden Jacobs-Jenkins's searing family drama, similarly resonated with audiences as a modern masterpiece, powered by Sarah Paulson's commanding presence and an ensemble firing on all cylinders.

The season also showcased Broadway's expanding theatrical vocabulary. **Stranger Things: The First Shadow** arrived from London's West End with jaw-dropping technical wizardry that proved big-budget spectacle could coexist with substantive storytelling. Meanwhile, solo shows like **Just for Us** demonstrated the enduring power of one performer, a microphone, and a compelling story—in Alex Edelman's case, his hilarious and unsettling account of infiltrating a white nationalist meeting.

From **Parade**'s timely exploration of antisemitism to **Purlie Victorious**'s bracingly relevant satire of racism, from **Fat Ham**'s Pulitzer-winning Hamlet riff to Jodie Comer's tour de force in **Prima Facie**, 2023's plays tackled urgent social issues without sacrificing entertainment value. Musical revivals like **Sweeney Todd** and newcomers like **Buena Vista Social Club** rounded out a season that offered something for every theatergoer.

Whether you're planning your next Broadway visit or simply exploring what you missed, these ten productions represent the best of what 2023's theatrical landscape had to offer.

best-broadway-plays-2026.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays Opening in 2026

As Broadway moves through March 2026, the year's theatrical landscape is just beginning to take shape with intimate, affecting productions that prioritize emotional connection over spectacle.

Leading the early arrivals is **Every Brilliant Thing**, which marks Daniel Radcliffe's return to Broadway in a decidedly unconventional format. This interactive solo show tackles depression and resilience through the lens of life's small pleasures, with Radcliffe breaking the fourth wall to engage audiences directly in the storytelling. Critics have responded warmly to his performance, awarding the production an 81/100 average across 25 reviews and consistently praising his ability to navigate the show's delicate tonal balance between humor and heartbreak.

The production represents a notable shift from Radcliffe's previous Broadway outings, stripping away ensemble casts and elaborate staging in favor of raw, direct communication with theatergoers. This approach has resonated particularly well with critics who appreciate the show's accessibility and emotional honesty, though the interactive elements mean each performance varies depending on audience participation.

With only one major play opening thus far in 2026, the year remains wide open for new productions to make their mark. The strong critical reception for *Every Brilliant Thing* sets a high bar for intimacy and authenticity, suggesting that audiences may be gravitating toward smaller, more personal theatrical experiences. As the spring season progresses, theater enthusiasts should watch for announcements of additional productions that will fill out the year's roster.
